No, this analysis is not defensible as fit.

The model lmer(rt ~ condition + (1 | subject)) is missing a by-subject random slope for condition — and condition is a within-subjects manipulation, which makes this omission consequential, not just a simplification.

Why it matters: When condition varies within subjects (each person sees both levels), the correct error term for testing the condition effect is the by-subject variability in how much condition affects RT. A random-intercepts-only model doesn't estimate that variability; it pools residual variance incorrectly and produces a test statistic that is anti-conservative — the denominator of the F/t ratio is too small. The result is inflated Type I error. Barr, Levy, Scheepers & Tily (2013) — 'Keep It Maximal' — and Schielzeth & Forstmeier (2009) both document this: false-positive rates for within-subjects effects can reach 20–50% at nominal α = .05 when the by-subject slope is omitted.

The p = 0.02 finding is suspect precisely because the model is misconfigured for this design. The 'significant' result may be a false positive.

What to do: Refit with a by-subject random slope:

```r
model <- lmer(rt ~ condition + (1 + condition | subject), data = d)
```

If that model produces a singular fit warning (common with small N or few levels), follow the convergence troubleshooting workflow — try scaling predictors, switching to sum coding, or using allFit() — before reflexively dropping the slope back out.

Bottom line: report the refit model, not the current one. A p-value from a misspecified model isn't a finding you can defend at review.
